script:
Ever wonder why a philosopher drank poison on stage?

Okay, so this is Jacques‑Louis David’s 1787 canvas, The Death of Socrates. He painted it in oil on a massive 129 × 196 cm sheet, and every brushstroke screams drama. The scene? Socrates, sentenced by Athens, chooses hemlock over exile, while his followers watch, stunned. Look at Socrates right there, calm as a monk, his right hand holding the cup—he’s about to sip his fate. Plato’s peering up, eyes wide, like “no way this is happening.” Over on the left, Crito clutches his own cup, maybe ready to share the drink. And that guy on the far right? He’s the servant with a second cup, a subtle nod that the ritual is public. Notice the tiny lyre tucked in the lower right corner—David slipped it in to hint at the harmony lost when philosophy dies. Also, the hemlock cup is tilted, showing the poison spilling, a visual cue of inevitable death. So next time you see a philosopher with a cup, ask yourself: would you sip or stand aside?
